body: Proton and Windscribe are two of the most recommended VPNs available right now, but which should you buy?
Proton is one of our best VPNs: a heavily audited privacy player with an encrypted ecosystem you can use alongside, while Windscribe packs huge amounts of functionality for power users.

This year’s Black Friday deals make the choice trickier: Proton’s two-year VPN Plus plan is down to $2.49/month (75% off), while Windscribe Pro is $2.42/month with a 58% discount. Below, we compare the paid plans on features, security, speed, and price.
Proton VPN vs Windscribe: Features
Proton’s cheapest tier is VPN Plus, and it’s purely a VPN. Step up to Proton Unlimited, and you also get Proton Mail Plus, Proton Pass, 500 GB of encrypted Drive storage, and Premium calendar.

Windscribe takes the opposite approach with one flat Pro plan. You get R.O.B.E.R.T. – a highly customizable DNS-level blocker for ads, trackers, and malware – plus port forwarding, optional static IPs, and full custom configuration generators for WireGuard, OpenVPN, and IKEv2.

As far as core VPN tech goes, both obfuscate traffic with proprietary protocols – Proton’s Stealth and Windscribe’s WStunnel. Multihop comes in two forms: Proton’s Secure Core routes you through hardened servers in privacy-friendly jurisdictions like Iceland. Windscribe’s Double Hop lets you hand-pick any two locations. Proton additionally offers VPN Accelerator, which claims to speed up connections by processing traffic more efficiently, and alternative routing for censored networks.

On security and privacy, Proton VPN Plus puts up the stronger front: NetShield blocks ads, trackers, and malware at the DNS level, Tor-over-VPN servers let you browse the Tor network without the Tor Browser, the apps are open-source, and the no-logs policy has been repeatedly audited – all backed by Swiss jurisdiction.

Windscribe’s apps are open source too, and its VPN server infrastructure underwent independent security and penetration testing by PacketLabs in June 2024. The assessment examined its no-logs implementation, identified some logging issues, and a subsequent retest confirmed those issues had been fixed.
Its R.O.B.E.R.T. ad, tracker, and malware blocker also deserves mentioning, especially since it performed better than NetShield in our most recent testing.

Where Windscribe also leads is future-proofing: since October 2025, its desktop and mobile apps have offered post-quantum encryption on WireGuard connections. Proton has no equivalent yet, though it’s on the roadmap.

Although they rank among the fastest VPNs, our latest testing favored Windscribe at home and Proton abroad: on WireGuard, Windscribe hit 2054 Mbps locally versus Proton’s 1783 Mbps, but Proton was faster on a US-to-UK connection (1397 Mbps vs Windscribe's 1284 Mbps).

For streaming, both cracked multiple Netflix regions – including US, UK and Canada – Disney+ (occasionally on a second attempt), BBC iPlayer, and 9Now. However, Proton failed with ITVX and TVNZ+, which Windscribe handled, while Windscribe failed with YouTube US. Unfortunately, both couldn't access Prime Video across multiple countries.
Proton VPN vs Windscribe: Pricing

Proton VPN’s headline deal this Black Friday is VPN Plus over two years at $2.49/month, down 75% from the usual $9.99/month. This is billed as $59.76 upfront for 24 months before it renews at $83.88 every 12 months. Its Unlimited one-year plan is 50% off at $6.49/month, billed as $77.88 for the first 12 months before renewing at $119.88 every 12 months.

Windscribe’s Black Friday sale takes Pro from its usual $5.75/month to $2.42/month (58% off), billed as $29 every 12 months. Crucially, Windscribe renews at that same $29/year instead of jumping to a higher rate.

For the first year, it’s effectively a tie: $29/year for Windscribe versus $29.88/year for Proton Plus. At renewal, Windscribe stays at $29/year while Proton plans roughly double. Rather not commit long-term? Proton VPN Plus is $9.99/month, Unlimited $12.99/month, and Windscribe Pro $9.00/month.

Windscribe also lets you build your own plan at $1/month per location ($3 minimum, up to seven countries), which is great if you only need one or two countries year-round, though you’re limited to 10GB of data per location (an extra $1/month buys unlimited data and access R.O.B.E.R.T. access). The two providers offer free tiers too, but they’re much more limited.

With Windscribe, you can enjoy unlimited simultaneous connections. Proton caps simultaneous connections at 10 devices, which is nothing to sniff at, but may prove limiting for households with lots of devices.
Platform coverage is broadly matched: both ship polished Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Apple TV, and Fire TV apps, plus browser extensions.

Proton has the much friendlier refund policy. It offers a full 30-day money-back guarantee versus Windscribe’s much shorter 7-day window, which comes with a catch: you must have used less than 10GB of data.
Verdict
Proton VPN Plus is the winner here. Its no-logs promise is independently audited and backed by Swiss jurisdiction.

With this Black Friday deal, it’s effectively the same price as Windscribe Pro. Proton’s one cause for pause is the renewal: it jumps to $83.88/year once the deal ends, while Windscribe stays at $29/year indefinitely.
Choose Proton if you want the privacy-focused all-rounder – or Unlimited if you’ll use Proton Pass and Drive daily.
Opt for Windscribe if unlimited devices, port forwarding, or post-quantum WireGuard matter most, or if you’re settling in for the long haul and prefer to avoid a hefty renewal bill.

body: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.

According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.

Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.
Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.
Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

articles.headline: JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source
keyFacts: JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.
The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.

Like its predecessor , Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language , in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use.
body: JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.
The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.

Like its predecessor , Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language , in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files.
Dirty data

The revised benchmar k now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories.

The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request.
A 30-minute limit was set for each task.

Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60 percent on those based on closed source repositories.

Although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely new to them.
Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks.
Leaderboard Shakeup

When restricted to closed source tasks, two dark horse models rose to the top: Gemini 3.8 Flash, via Antigravity CLI, topped the list with a 60 percent success rate, closely followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (running on OpenCode) at 58.9 percent.
Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however.

In contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models.
Claude’s lackluster completion rates on closed source tasks are somewhat sus given how both of these Anthropic models scored significantly higher on tasks using open source materials.
In fact Claude ran the table when it came to open source: Fable 5.1 topped the charts with 86.2 percent accuracy, closely followed by Opus 5.5 at 84.8 percent accuracy.
(Kotlin users will pay dearly for the extra sliver of Anthropic accuracy: The average cost of Fable completing a Kotlin cleanup task runs $2.38, while Opus could do the job for $0.68.)
Gaming the boss

One possible interpretation of these disparate numbers is that models are drawing from their own knowledge bases instead of reasoning from scratch. Whether this is cheating or the models simply working as intended might be more a matter of philosophical debate.
Mark Hinkle, founder of the AIE Network consultancy, suspects the issue of integrity may go deeper.
"Private code doesn't stop reward hacking, it changes the shortcut," he wrote to The Register on LinkedIn.

"On public code the agent goes and finds the answer somebody has already published. On private code there's no answer to find, so it satisfies whatever is checking it. I treat these things like entry-level employees, and a sharp new hire figures out fast what the boss actually looks at."

JetBrains did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but concluded in its post that more investigation is needed. It promises that its people will pore over the open source results to see if any have been contaminated by the LLMs' own memory. It also plans to run its own static analysis tool, Qodana , against the results to check for errors.
Sireesha Pulipati , a staff data engineer and AI observer, suggested, also by LinkedIn, that JetBrains may have needed more specificity in its agent instructions.

"Out of the box [an agent] tends to reach for generic patterns. But when we give it instructions and skills that tell it where to look for our patterns and context, it follows them. A well-controlled harness, with those standards built in, is what makes the agent useful," Pulipati wrote.
So good on JetBrains for providing Kotlin users some information about working with AI, but, as always, AI benchmarks should be approached with extreme side-eye. ®

articles.headline: I'm having a much better time in GTA 6 now I've disabled its pesky Criminal Profile pings
keyFacts: Do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life?
You crouch to fuss your dog, and a little ping activates in your retina, informing you that you've just earned plus-three serotonin.
Your boss chews you out for coming into work 15 minutes late thanks to a traffic accident holding you up on your way to work, a notification pings: "-10 percent motivation (lasts 24 hours)".
body: Do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life? You crouch to fuss your dog, and a little ping activates in your retina, informing you that you've just earned plus-three serotonin. Your boss chews you out for coming into work 15 minutes late thanks to a traffic accident holding you up on your way to work, a notification pings: "-10 percent motivation (lasts 24 hours)". Maybe you eat a bang-up meal, flirt with a hot stranger, beat your personal best on a run - ding, ding, ding. Well done, you win at being a human.

I think it'd be tortuous. I think it would interact with my already-questionable perception of reality, and send my neurodivergent coping mechanisms into overdrive. I already see time 'in blocks', and am incapable of breaking tasks down to anything less than 15 minute chunks - I can't imagine how ill I'd get if I could begin ascribing status buffs and debuffs to those blocks, too. We're all different, of course - such is the beauty of life - but I think most people would be pushed to the point of meltdown if every action they took had a quantifiable mechanical system attached to it.

So why is it any different in GTA 6? The game, after all, is the most effective simulation we've ever seen about modern life. Aside from the rampant crime sprees you can engage with, there's so much mundanity in the game it's beyond impressive: I spent the opening 10-or-so hours in the game with a very strict morning routine. I'd get up, work out, shower, feed Dolores the snake, drink a protein shake, then head to one of the local businesses to get some breakfast. Every day! I'm a busy person; I'm playing GTA 6 for fun, yes, but also as part of my job - I need to be making progress. Yet, Rockstar's invisible hand is so competently realised, so artisanally implemented, that I bow to its insistence that I live life properly and engage with all the systems suggested to me like a good little drone.

So, after being low-key brainwashed by the initial tutorialisation, it stands to reason that I'm open to Rockstar's other suggestions. And - right on cue - you get a mission early on that introduces you to what is perhaps the most hotly debated aspect of the game so far: the Criminal Profile. If you're unaware, this new mechanic is a bit like the Honour System in Red Dead Redemption 2. It's broken down into five levels: professional, hardened, violent, psycho, and irredeemable. If you hit that final bracket, irredeemable, you can never go back: it's essentially GTA 6's criminal version of 'being cancelled', only here there are real, serious consequences that will actually ruin your life forever.

The game tracks how you behave when you're playing as both Jason and Lucia. They have separate criminal profiles. If, for example, you fudge a robbery on a cartel's pill-shipping operation and fight for your life, you can certainly kill everyone in the room - that's still fine. This is still Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar isn't trying to make you play this game like Thief or Deus Ex or something. You can go for total stealth runs, but incapacitating enemies without killing them and getting away cleanly will only grant 'professional' points. You get the same assessment if you 'go loud' and aim for the hands, knees, feet of the people trying to kill you. I am currently about 30 hours in, and every single encounter has been either 'no casualties' or 'low casualties', and I promise I've not even been trying that hard to 'be good' (and there are always settings you can change to help you out if you're struggling, too).

There has been a certain amount of online discourse pointing towards this system as 'immersion ruining' or 'systematically inhibiting'. There's this idea that, in order to get a number of the game's 'good' endings, you need to play like a saint the whole way through the game. This is untrue. It's actually weighted more towards the opposite: in order to get the more nefarious ranks, you need to intentionally play like a sociopath. Wing a goon, see him lying on the floor in agony, and then go over and shoot his other kneecap? Yeah, you're going to get those unpopular purple devil points. Kick a dog in the street for no reason? Devil points. Taking a shotgun to a mall and opening fire on unarmed, un-implicated civilians? Devil points.

I'm enjoying the role-playing aspect of the game, because in my head-canon Jason and Lucia are doing what they can to survive. It may not be pretty, and I probably wouldn't want to know them in real life, but - as far as this work of fiction goes - I think playing them as criminals-on-the-run, trying to draw as little attention to themselves as possible is a great iteration of the series' core themes. I don't want to play as another Tommy Vercetti, or CJ, or Trevor. I want something different, and this game is giving it to me.

"The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper," explains Michael Wiafe, writer at Rockstar, in materials shared with Eurogamer ahead of the game's release. "[They're] full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn’t necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don’t attempt to make excuses for them. What’s important is how they resonate, no matter where you’re experiencing the game in the world." I think this shows, quite well, what the Criminal Profile mechanic sets out to achieve in GTA 6: it's Rockstar saying 'these people are forced into certain situations by us, the developers, but you get to figure out how they respond to what life is giving them'.

And you know what? I'm glad GTA 6 punishes you for playing like a psychopath. The world of Leonida is analogous to the real world, and things would start going wrong for you if you started attacking pedestrians randomly on the street. Other civilians and cops would start defending themselves and resisting you if you instigated a rampage of indiscriminate violence. The only time I've been victim to the devil icon in my game so far is when a Kingfisher accidentally shot out my (very expensive) windshield whilst aiming for Jason. So I kneecapped him, stole his beer, drank the whole bottle, then threw the bottle at his head. I acted like an idiot, and got treated as such. Good!

But I don't want to see that. I want to roleplay as Jason and Lucia and act as I think they would. I don't need the game telling me, like a little voice in my head, 'hm, actually, that was a pretty weird thing to do, we're going to write that down'. So I have turned the notifications off. It's a simple process: simply open Settings, and then navigate to UI, and head down to the 34/70 area and you'll see all the HUD notifications settings. I play with both Criminal Profile and Relationship settings turned off - I prefer to have all that happening in the background, ticking over as I play, rather than constantly reminding me there's some secret meter somewhere judging me for what I'm doing.

If my relationship is turning sour, I trust my instincts (and Rockstar's grounded, well-structured writing) to tell me that. Jason is getting a bit cold, Lucia doesn't want to jump my bones, like, all the time, the two aren't holding hands at every opportunity like lovesick puppies… Much like in my real-life relationships, I trust the process. And I think more people should, because the role-playing in this game is fantastic, and we've been given a real rich text to engage with. I think that the fact that certain corners of the internet are upset because they're being treated badly for being bad people is a better level of satire than anything GTA 6 has put in-game, to be honest.

body: The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) unveiled new tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including the European Union and China.
A senior US official said the proposed duties follow a months-long investigation into allegations that excessive manufacturing abroad puts American producers at a disadvantage.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the proposed tariffs largely stick to rates set under existing trade agreements, although some could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.

China would face an additional tariff of 20%, bringing the combined rate for some Chinese goods to 45%. The proposed duties would respect the 15% tariff cap agreed with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, according to a senior US administration official.
Other affected economies include India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam.
The tariffs could take effect in January at the earliest, following a public comment period.
Why is Trump planning new tariffs?
The measures are also intended to replace revenues lost after the US Supreme Court struck down US president Donald Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February.

The proposed duties could further fuel US inflation, which reached 3.7% in September. High living costs were a key issue in November's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress.
The tariff plans come just weeks before Trump is due to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.
The US official played down concerns about renewed trade tensions and said Washington could sign further trade agreements at the summit.

articles.headline: Effective altruism is ceding America’s AI edge to China
keyFacts: Anthropic leaders founded the company on the effective altruism ideology and are lobbying in Washington to influence American artificial intelligence policies.
The author states that effective altruism has a history marked by financial fraud, misconduct scandals, and connections to controversial figures.
The article claims that effective altruism policies, such as chip export controls, prioritize hypothetical future risks over competing with China.
body: By now, it is undeniable that artificial intelligence will decide which country sets the terms of the next century. The United States currently holds the lead in both the software and the chips that power it. But that measurable lead is not guaranteed. One company, Anthropic, is investing in millions for political capital in Washington, D.C., to slow the very American capabilities that keep us ahead. They do this by wrapping the effort in the language of a left-wing, cult-like ideology known as “effective altruism.”

Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI executives who present their mission as making AI more reliable and controlled. Founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rooted the company in effective altruism, whose core claims favor neat quantitative models and scientific calculations to decide what is best for the world.

But the world, as we know it, runs on more than just science and data, and its perverted emphasis on using science to judge what is best for humanity has repeatedly failed to make contact with reality.

Effective altruism’s most famous public face, Sam Bankman-Fried, used the “earn to give” slogan as cover while orchestrating one of the largest financial frauds in American history. Leaders in the community were warned about his conduct years earlier and still accepted tens of millions for EA causes. Anthropic itself drew early capital from Bankman-Fried’s circle and from other major EA funders. When Dario Amodei has described the principle that “no bad person should ever profit from our success” as difficult to follow in business, the tension is obvious. According to the Financial Times , Bankman-Fried, as Anthropic’s early investor, would have made up to $43 billion from its recent IPO, highlighting the moral hypocrisy of Anthropic steeped in effective altruism.

Calling effective altruism cult-like is also not hyperbole. It is documented reality. In the Bay Area, EA overlaps directly with a Berkeley-based community that has been described as operating like a sex cult, intellectually anchored by Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of EA’s leading intellects. Shared donors, employers, social networks, and communal housing bind this group together, where apocalyptic warnings about AI extinction serve to attract devoted young recruits, donations, and policy leverage. Reporting has documented communal living, polyamorous relationships, and allegations of abuse involving housing dependence, financial vulnerability, drugs, and unequal power.

Separately, seven women told Time magazine they experienced sexual harassment and misconduct within EA’s overwhelmingly male, professionally incestuous subculture. Julia Wise, the longest-serving employee of the Centre for Effective Altruism, has acknowledged reports of sexual harassment within the community. Add in EA’s obsession with “community building” and youth recruitment programs such as LEAF in England, and the picture is unmistakable: These are not the people who should be setting America’s technology policy.

But effective altruists have already penetrated the country’s political system through Anthropic as its main vehicle. Anthropic’s leadership and major backers have directed substantial sums to Democratic candidates and committees, including large contributions aligned with the 2024 presidential race. Former Biden administration national-security staff now hold senior roles shaping the company’s public policy positions about AI. Unsurprisingly, several of these individuals have ties to effective altruism, with Anthropic’s Head of National Security, Tarun Chhabra, and adviser, Ben Buchanan, having worked at EA-funded institutions.

Beyond influencing politics, EA has already undermined America’s global competition with China. Highlighting hypothetical, far-off sci-fi catastrophes caused by AI over the real-world economic and security needs of America today, its adherents have relentlessly lobbied for sweeping export controls on advanced U.S. chips, claiming they would set China back by years. Even inside the EA-influenced think tank world, those claims have collapsed: RAND researcher Lennart Heim admitted in 2023 that export controls set China back closer to 10% — not years — while RAND employees themselves have warned that EA’s radical philosophy is eroding the institution’s credibility. Yet, these ideological zealots keep pushing short-sighted restrictions that scare American firms and allies from maximizing this tech while China charges ahead with its “AI Plus” strategy.
HOW BEIJING’S AI PUSH FUELS A GLOBAL PIPELINE FOR SMUGGLED NVIDIA CHIPS

Effective altruism’s tunnel vision of the world treats the present’s economic and security needs as secondary to hypothetical future risks. That ordering is a political choice, not one grounded in reality. America’s interests are straightforward: maintain the lead in frontier models and advanced chips, embed those capabilities with partners who share our security goals, and prevent firms steeped in radical ideologies from ceding our lead to China. Policymakers should treat Anthropic’s recommendations as the product of an unrealistic ideology with documented past fraud and a record of overstated claims.
Slowing American progress to satisfy a dubious philosophy is a choice we do not have to make.

Matt Mackowiak is the president of Potomac Strategy Group, served in the Bush administration at the Department of Homeland Security, on the Bush-Cheney reelection campaign, and was a senior communications aide to three U.S. Senators and a Governor.

articles.headline: Sneako asked who created the Taliban. He should have asked who pays for its rule
keyFacts: On Monday, Jensen Huang got his job back.
Sneako said he still hadn’t gotten his phone back.
Nvidia reinstated Huang as chief executive, and Wall Street rallied.
body: On Monday, Jensen Huang got his job back. Sneako said he still hadn’t gotten his phone back. Nvidia reinstated Huang as chief executive, and Wall Street rallied. The American livestreamer, meanwhile, told his audience that federal agents questioned him for eight hours on his way home from Afghanistan and took his phone and other devices. He said the FBI was examining them. Federal authorities had yet to publicly confirm his account.

The phone brought the story back to America. The most revealing moment was already on camera in Afghanistan. In one widely shared clip, Sneako asks a man whether America created the Taliban . The man rejects the premise and credits Afghans with founding the movement. An American had traveled halfway around the world to ask an Afghan about his country, and the question still managed to give America the starring role.

Americans should argue about our own conduct in Afghanistan . We backed Afghan fighters against the Soviet Union in the 1980s, and some veterans of that war later joined the Taliban. But the movement took shape in the 1990s during an Afghan civil war and received support from Pakistan. Those distinctions matter because different people made different decisions at different times. If the whole story begins and ends in Washington, the men who built the Taliban are somehow relieved of responsibility for building it. The man in the clip was willing to claim more agency than the question allowed him. I wish Sneako had taken him at his word and pressed him on what that agency entails.

Israel gets assigned a similarly implausible role in online explanations of political violence. If you start with the belief that Israel is behind every act of terrorism, you can spare yourself the trouble of learning what a particular movement believes, whom it recruits, what it wants, and whom it harms. You also lose any reason to listen when the people you’re speaking to give you an answer you didn’t expect.

In a separate clip, Taliban figure Anas Haqqani invokes the rights of Christians and Jews when asked about perceptions of Islam. Anyone waiting for him to say Jews should be killed would have been disappointed by that answer. As a Jew, I’m glad viewers heard him say what he did. I’d also have liked to hear a follow-up. Which rights would he defend for people who disagree with his government? Would they be free to say so in public? What would happen to an Afghan journalist who pressed him on the gap between that assurance and the way the Taliban governs?

Craig Considine’s new book, When Marx Meets Islam: Navigating Radical Ideologies in Defense of the West , helps explain why some audiences might find an unscripted answer so unwelcome. The Rice University sociologist argues that some revolutionary leftists and Islamist movements can make common cause against America and Israel while wanting profoundly different societies. Considine, who has spent years working on Christian-Muslim relations, says he experienced the cost of departing from that common line when he supported the Abraham Accords. “They tried to silence me for defending peace,” he said when the book came out.

Think about what he was defending. The accords gave people in Israel and Arab countries a chance to build relationships that generations of politics had made difficult. A person who has spent years advocating interfaith engagement had every reason to welcome that opportunity. If supporting it made some of his former allies doubt his loyalties, it’s worth asking what they expected him to be loyal to. An Afghan who refuses to blame America for his own side’s decisions creates a similar problem for people who were counting on him to do exactly that.

Ruth Wasserman Lande, a former Israeli deputy ambassador to Egypt, has written about how governments can “filter the messages to which their publics are exposed.” She was talking about the information that audiences in parts of the Arab world receive about Israel. Her observation applies to Americans watching a livestream from Kabul, too. Every trip has people who open doors, people who decide which doors stay closed, and people with good reasons to keep their heads down. An influencer may get better access than a journalist. That can make what he films more interesting. It makes it even more important to ask whose interests the access serves.

Here’s the interview I wanted to see. Give an Afghan girl who finished sixth grade the same time you give a Taliban official. Ask her what she was good at in school. Ask what she hoped to do afterward, what her parents expected for her, and what she does now with the hours she used to spend in class. Under Taliban rule, girls are barred from secondary education beyond sixth grade. A girl living under that policy can tell you things about her country that a government official has every incentive to leave out. She deserves to be heard on terms that protect her safety.

Then go back to the official who spoke about rights and ask him to explain that policy. Ask him when she can go back to school. If his answer is that she can’t, ask him why he thinks he has the right to make that decision for her. That is the point at which an interview earns the access it was given.
SEWARD’S SECOND BARGAIN: LOCK GREENLAND, FREE THE FAROE ISLANDS, AND END NORWAY’S SURRENDER OF SVALBARD

I want federal authorities to establish what happened on the trip and act if there is evidence of unlawful conduct. If the facts and the law support deportation and the government proves its case through due process, I would support it. The public record has yet to establish that basis. Sneako’s account of what happened to his phone leaves the public with questions about what agents examined, what they found, and whether any law was broken. Those questions deserve answers grounded in evidence.

The part of this story I keep coming back to is the man who interrupted an American’s theory about Afghanistan with an answer about Afghanistan. Sneako could have followed that exchange wherever it led. He could have asked the people who claim credit for building the Taliban to explain, in their own words, what they owe the people who live under it. I’d start by asking when that girl gets to go back to school.
Warren H. Cohn is the founder and CEO of RocketshipPR and a media adviser to the American Middle East Press Association.

body: What next for Ferrari after Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton's latest collision with No 1 driver and consequences up for debate

Listen to the latest edition of The F1 Show podcast as Simon Lazenby, David Croft and Jamie Chadwick debate what's next at Ferrari after another driver clash; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
Wednesday 25 November 2026 14:16, UK

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton's latest run-in at the Las Vegas Grand Prix has ramped up scrutiny on Ferrari and what the team will do to try to avoid more costly on-track incidents between their two drivers.

Just two races after a fierce battle when running first and second on the opening lap in Mexico City cost the team victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen and led to clear-the-air discussions, the team-mates collided when battling over sixth place in Las Vegas in an incident Leclerc was found at fault for by the stewards and then received the post-race ire of team boss Frederic Vasseur.

Vasseur has said such incidents "cannot continue" but how does the Frenchman get on top of the situation heading towards 2027, when the team will be hoping to launch a fresh bid to end what stands as an 18-year world title drought?

The Ferrari fallout proved a central topic on the latest edition of Sky Sports' The F1 Show podcast ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, in which host Simon Lazenby was joined by David Croft and Jamie Chadwick.
Asked how big the problems between Hamilton and Leclerc were becoming for Ferrari, Chadwick said: "Significant when you think about what they're going to potentially be going into next year with.

"I think this is the time of the year where you don't want to be having these kinds of conflicts because suddenly it will escalate and it will mean that more serious conversation is going to be had in the background."
So what might Ferrari do next?
Impose a No 1 driver?

Former world champion Damon Hill recently said he believed Ferrari should make Hamilton, the seven-time world champion and F1's most successful driver, their clear No 1 next year if they want to win the world championship.

Speaking on Sky Sports F1 after Sunday's incident in Las Vegas, Jacques Villeneuve, the 1997 title winner, suggested Leclerc - who is in his eighth season with the Scuderia - had "lost" the leadership of the team to Hamilton, who is in his second, and "if there's one of the two drivers knows how to win championships, it's Lewis".
Villeneuve did, however, question whether Ferrari would be able to prioritise Hamilton contractually.

Hamilton said after the race that he has "never asked" for No 1 status at the team, although implied they could have given him more backing when he was second to Kimi Antonelli and around 40 points ahead of Leclerc in the championship earlier this season.

And although Hamilton and Leclerc are both among the sport's biggest names and most-talented drivers, Croft believes events of this season have effectively forced the team's hand and they need to prioritise one over the other in order to achieve better results.
"Whether Lewis Hamilton is asking to be No 1 or not, I don't think matters any more," said Croft.
"I think the way things have panned out this season the matter has been forced.
"Lewis has to be the No 1 because Charles keeps putting himself in a position whereby Ferrari suffer when the two drivers come together.

"He got the penalty on Sunday. Whether you think it's a penalty or not, the move was ambitious and it was ambitious if it was a move on Lando Norris, it was ambitious and a bit foolish if it's a move on your own team-mate.

"So Charles is kind of forcing, albeit not deliberately, Ferrari to make these decisions. He did race Lewis hard in Mexico City, and we saw what happened there, and he raced Lewis hard in Monza, and we saw what happened there."
Long regarded as one of the fastest drivers in the sport, Leclerc, 29, is a graduate of Ferrari's academy and joined their race team in 2019 after a debut season of F1 at Sauber.

He outperformed four-time champion Sebastian Vettel and then Carlos Sainz across their respective seasons as team-mates and was comfortably ahead of Hamilton by over 80 points after the Briton joined from Mercedes last year.
But Leclerc has faced a resurgent force in Hamilton this year, with the 41-year-old holding a 17-point advantage over him in the championship with two races to go.
"Charlie's a fine driver, don't get me wrong, but his pole-to-win conversion rate (27 to nine) is not enough," added Croft on Leclerc's Ferrari record so far.
"You can also argue that the team haven't given him the car to make that conversion rate better, but he does make mistakes, we've seen that.

"We've seen in the past when he's been leading a race and he's crashed out all by himself. He's not the finished article and I don't want to be too harsh on Charles, I think he's a truly wonderful human being, but he's no Lewis Hamilton when it comes to his record and his performances and his consistency over the years."
Enforce firmer rules and consequences?
Vasseur said he would hold fresh discussions with his drivers this week.
But do those talks need to now go further in terms of setting out firmly what is and is not acceptable - and establishing consequences for any transgressions?
Chadwick said: "I think the biggest issue [to this point] is the conversations haven't been serious enough.

"I think a clear-the-air talk as in 'okay it's not your fault, it's not your fault' and 'okay this is how things are' versus, actually, what are the rules of engagement? What are the reprimands if you do take your team-mate out and are they severe enough that actually neither driver is going to dare put themselves in that position?

"Clearly not because when you look at the move Charles did. Okay I kind of agree a little bit it wasn't not on, but it's definitely not on on your team-mate. I think you can maybe risk a move like Lando did on Lewis and I think that's also actually where Charles was a bit unlucky [in that he] went for it and then he kind of sees the door closing a bit and then he backs out and then it's kind of worse because he's over the kerb and that's what caused him to hit him.

"If he had actually just really committed to it maybe it would have been a bit better but, either way, you just never do that on your team-mate and clearly he didn't see there being any risk as to making a move like that on his team-mate. In his mind in that moment, Lewis is the same as any other driver on that grid. it's not a car in the same team as you.
"So that definitely needs a lot of discussion behind the scenes."
Chadwick, though, believes it is possible to win world titles with two No 1 drivers.
"I think it can still work with two drivers of top calibre but there has to be clear rules of engagement," she added.
"That's what we were arguably critical of, but it worked for McLaren last year."
Or will anything change at all?

But given the repeat nature of the on-track clashes and flashpoints between Hamilton and Leclerc this season, Croft is unsure much will actually change despite the incident and another round of discussions.
"So what do Ferrari do?" pondered Croft.

"They either say 'Lewis is No 1 going forward' and 'sorry, Charles, you're not going to get involved with this and you're working for your team-mate because we need a championship here'. Or they get a new team principal who can actually maybe have a better sway over the two drivers, because at the moment it looks like whatever Fred says it just gets ignored out on track. Or they can just carry on as they are doing.

"And if I was going to put whatever dollars you had left over from Vegas on this one, I'd probably say Ferrari are just going to carry on and do what they did this year next year as well because they've had every chance so far this year to actually address the situation and they've not addressed it right so far."

articles.headline: Any official GTA 6 PC port’s ability to deliver a proper first person mode would be its biggest ace in the hole, so reckon I, a traitor
keyFacts: To be fair, I’ve made no secret of my plans to do just that if you’ve read any of our recent roundups of what everyone’s playing over the weekend.
I can understand why it might leave a sour taste in the mouth, but it is what it is.
No corporate gun has been pointed at my head as a mandate to temporarily forsake my PC and play the big game of the moment is forced into my hands.
body: I’ve been playing GTA 6 on PS5.

To be fair, I’ve made no secret of my plans to do just that if you’ve read any of our recent roundups of what everyone’s playing over the weekend. I can understand why it might leave a sour taste in the mouth, but it is what it is. No corporate gun has been pointed at my head as a mandate to temporarily forsake my PC and play the big game of the moment is forced into my hands.

Anyway, I’m writing about playing GTA 6 on console because it’s led me to conclude that a particular aspect of GTA 5’s PC port - one I’ve always rather taken for granted - could be a bigger deal for the inevitable Windows version of 6 than even the usual go-to PC plus points. You know, better graphics, superior performance, and modding. Historically, Rockstar’s crime sandboxes are games played from the third person perspective. That shot lingering behind Niko Bellic as he jogs around Brooklyn with a rocket launcher or following the damn bike of CJ as he in turn follows that damn train. This is the default way GTA’s breakneck action is presented to the player and was with GTA 5 at launch.

As Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into. In order to do that, while simultaneously pushing the detail and graphical boundaries of their rendered worlds, Rockstar have needed to squeeze every bit of juice they can from the available hardware. Red Dead Redemption 2 managed to include a full first person mode at launch. GTA 6 hasn’t been so lucky, even if there are moments when bringing up your phone or reading a note temporarily lodges the camera into Jason and Lucia’s noggins.

There is a way to glitch yourself into a more permanent first person perspective, but it’s naturally not got the polish that a proper first person mode would. What it does do is make clear that, with vehicle interiors lavishly detailed and some gun animations looking natural rather than janky, any port using the PC's extra horses to deliver a proper first person mode seems a no brainer, if not something already set in stone.

Assuming that is the case, I frankly can’t see why first person won’t become the go-to perspective on PC. Even more so than RDR2, GTA 6 feels like a game built to belong in first person. It dedicates so much time and energy to engaging you in every aspect of Jason and Lucia’s routines, rendering everything from eating to working out to doing up a house (and the acts involved in doing a robbery, I guess) in such exhaustive detail and depth that it’s almost beyond parody.

Notifications ping about you needing to finish a bench pressing session where every rep involves holding and releasing R2 and L2 at just the right time. An app tells you you’re hungry, so you wander over to the fridge, pick out a protein shake to down, then press R2 to lob the bottle in the bin, assuming you’re keen to keep your flat tidy. Shopping trips see you pick up groceries off shelves, stow them in a bag, then run home with it tucked under your arm because you’ve brought a motorbike and forgotten it lacks a boot. Every stickup begins with the ritual of picking your longarm gun out of your car’s boot, where it might have sat next to a bag of drugs you’ve stowed to deliver to a fence later. Stopping off to switch cars and clothes to throw the cops off your scent is no longer just for overenthusiastic roleplayers.

The fact that the game goes to such lengths only to maintain the detachment inherent to the third person view feels bizarrely antithetical at times, like an exhibition of a tiny Fabergé egg that you’re forced to view through a telescope from the surface of Mars. The massive efforts of Rockstar’s developers - many of whom are currently trying to gain formal union recognition or have been fighting the company at an employment tribunal over firings they argue were unjust - went into putting together an artwork that regularly ends up at an arm’s length out of necessity, despite packing intricacies likely best seen through a magnifying glass.

Enter the PC release. And possibly nothing else offering the same bang for your buck around the same time. With GTA 5, the PS4 and Xbox One got an enhanced version of the game around the time of the PC port, offering a number of extra features - including a first person mode. Rockstar were quick to rule out GTA 6 getting 60 or 40fps performance modes on current console hardware due to a lack of horses, and if that also applies to a first person mode, then such a thing might only come with the next generation of consoles. That’d be the PS6 and Xbox’s Project Helix, neither of which seem hugely imminent and could well end up boasting ludicrous prices thanks to the ongoing memory shortages.

So, those who already own a PC capable of running any GTA 6 port could be in the best position to enjoy the game from a Jason and Lucia-eye view the moment such a thing becomes possible. Sure, it would also look and run better, but to be brutally honest I’ve found it looks damn gorgeous and runs acceptably on PS5. Sure, modding will no doubt spring up must-have additions, but the base game already works in plenty of the roleplaying mechanics and in-depth side-jobbing that a lot of popular GTA 5 mods delivered.

Thus, that window as the place to play GTA 6 as it feels intended, in first person, is what I’d currently peg as the best chance for the crimsim to be not just a great game you can play on PC - as I’d argue Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5 are - but a great PC game that’s inarguably best experienced on our platform of choice. I don’t think writing that is falling into the trap it’s easy to end up in with big games that hit console first: declaring in salesman-like fashion that they’ll of course be better on PC by default, in a manner that sometimes feels a bit like you’re trying to convince yourself that you’ve not paid more than a pre-RAM crisis console buyer for nothing.

I’d never consider playing Cyberpunk 2077 in anything but first person on PC. GTA 6, from what I’ve played thus far, could be the next uber-detailed open world I spend hundreds of hours taking in the sights of, ideally through the eyes of a highly dangerous and highly stylish operator on the prowl for lucrative underworld opportunities.

articles.headline: Trump proposes a new wave of tariffs on China, E.U. and other trade partners
keyFacts: The Trump administration proposed targeted tariffs on the European Union, China, and other partners over alleged unfair manufacturing practices.
China's commerce ministry rejected the tariffs, while talks with Canada continue due to outstanding sticking points.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer expects broad negotiations to follow before tariffs take effect in a couple of months.
body: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a new wave of tariffs on the European Union, China and other trade partners, the result of a probe into what it says are unfair manufacturing practices.

Some of the proposals include tariffs of at least 20% on China, which would match an agreement reached with the White House. But the duties could reach up to 40% if talks between the two countries fail.
The United States’ current trade truce with China was recently extended and is set to expire in January.

The tariffs will be implemented under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a statute that the White House has relied upon more frequently for trade authority ever since the Supreme Court blocked many of Trump’s 2025 country-specific tariffs, imposed under a different authority.

Wednesday’s announcement came less than a month after Trump’s tariff policies — and the inflation they fuel — contributed to Republicans’ sweeping losses in the U.S. midterm elections. Inflation hit 3.7% in September, driven primarily by energy prices but also by higher goods prices.

In announcing the details of the new duties, the U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the overall rates applied to each trading partner would not surpass levels that were previously agreed to as part of bilateral framework trade deals.
“When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points,” Greer said on CNBC.
“So what we’re proposing today are actually a set of targeted tariffs to respond to this problem of excess capacity,” he added.
For example, Trump agreed to cap tariffs on European Union imports at 15% as part of a deal reached in 2025. On Wednesday, the USTR reiterated that cap.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of existing duties, except for the case of China.

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this,” Greer said. “They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple of months from now.”
Greer said he expects that “a broad” negotiation with trading partners would follow today’s proposals.
But tensions continue to flare with trading partners, especially between Canada, the EU and China.

Overnight, a spokesperson for China’s commerce ministry rejected the basis for the new tariffs. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the ministry spokesperson said in a briefing for reporters.
“So-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false proposition,” they added. “China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”

Just weeks ago, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer accused the EU of “aggressively” supporting Airbus and said that a loan from the European Investment Bank to the French aerospace giant threatened to inject “substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector.”
The EU rejected Greer’s assertion, saying the loan was normal and he had “really no grounds” to question it. The bloc, made up of 27 countries, is the United States’ largest trading partner.
Meanwhile, in August, trade talks with Canada collapsed after Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trump administration requested “uneconomic” and unfair terms at the last minute.

Carney recalled his negotiators to Ottawa and for more than three months the two sides have traded verbal barbs. Canada is the country’s third largest trading partner, according to data through September of this year.
Recently, informal talks resumed between the U.S. and Canada but a formal deal does not yet appear to be within reach.
On Wednesday, Greer said those talks with Canada were continuing, due to some outstanding “sticking points.”
Another key U.S. trading partner, Mexico, was not included in Wednesday’s tariff proposals.

“I think the most important one where we’re still going through the investigation process, is Mexico,” Greer told CNBC. “I think it’ll be a little bit more time before we release that report,” he said.

Steelers upcoming schedule
The Steelers' schedule gets tougher before it eases up to finish the 2026 season.

For Rudolph, if he lasts three weeks or more as the starting quarterback, he'll be drawing some of the tougher matchups — and opposing defenses — of Pittsburgh's season. The 8-2 Broncos are first, a Denver team leading the AFC West behind another tough defense and opportunistic offense.

The Steelers will then get another home game against the Texans, who are currently 4-6 but still in the mix for the AFC wild-card chase. That "Sunday Night Football" matchup could have massive playoff consequences for Pittsburgh, either taking a big step back in the push or putting itself in position to finish the year strong.

From there, the schedule does favor the Steelers' path to the playoffs, facing a struggling Ravens squad led by Jacoby Brissett twice, along with games against the Panthers and Titans, both at .500 or worse right now.
Still, it's a brutal time for Rudolph to take over the offense.

body: Cristiano Ronaldo will achieve one of his most incredible individual feats when he finally reaches 1000 career goals in 2027.
The five-time Ballon d’Or winner is still hunting Golden Boot awards at his Saudi Arabian side, Al Nassr, months before his 42nd birthday.
Goal machine Ronaldo will reach a milestone by scoring his 1000th career goal in 2027 Getty
Ronaldo has made no secret of his desire to reach 1000 goals, something that has never been done in competitive football .
His fans have long since suspected that the former Portugal international wouldn’t hang up his boots until he hit the milestone.
However, his decision to follow rival Lionel Messi in stepping back from playing for his country , having played 234 times for Portugal, has narrowed his opportunities.
It means that Ronaldo can only edge closer to his career dream at club level, but the clock is ticking with Father Time against him.
The forward’s contract with Al Nassr expires next summer, and the man himself has admitted he expects it to be his last .
How many goals has Ronaldo scored?
Ronaldo scored his 987th career goal in a 2-1 AFC Champions League Elite win against Qatari side Al Sadd on Tuesday, November 24.
It was his 11th in 14 matches this season for Al Nassr in all competitions, having bagged 30 in 44 across the calendar year.
It means that Ronaldo, who scored three goals at the World Cup, has a scoring pace of roughly 0.75 to 0.79 goals per game in the 2026/27 season.
He is now just 13 goals away from 1000 in total.
Ronaldo confirmed that his 23-year international career is over, which leaves Al Nassr as his only route to hit 1,000 goals
When could he score his 1000th goal?
Barring any major injuries, Ronaldo is set to reach four figures for goals between mid-February and mid-March 2027 at his current rate.
Should the Manchester United legend go on a scoring streak and average a goal a game, then it would take him just 13 matches.
That would bring him up to potentially reach 1000 goals against Al-Taawou, on January 29, or a week later against Al-Shamal.
What’s more likely is that Ronaldo continues at his current pace, in which he will need 16 to 19 appearances to score 13 more goals.
The earlier end of that scale puts clashes with Shabab Al-Ahli (on February 15) or a home meeting with Al-Ittihad (on March 11).
Ronaldo took his season’s tally to 11 goals in 14 games across all competitions Getty
Ronaldo might be slightly delayed in his hunt by being left out of AFC Champions League away matches during the league phase.
He had no involvement in the 6-2 win against Uzbek side Pakhtakor at the start of November.
Ange Postecoglou’s men could add further games to Ronaldo’s schedule by advancing past the King’s Cup Round of 16 or reaching the AFC Champions League Elite knockout rounds.
Yet early exits might push his timeline back to around April, in which case fixtures against Al-Diriyah or Al-Ahli could be his crowning glory.
