Houthis renew threat to target Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports

The Iran-backed Houthis reiterated on Wednesday their threat to target Jeddah and all Saudi Arabian ports on the Red Sea if the Saudis follow through on their threat to target Yemen's Hodeidah port, which is held by the rebels.
Hodeidah is the main entry point for food and other essential supplies into Houthi-held northern Yemen.

In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree called on "employees and workers at these ports, as well as those present in their vicinity, to evacuate them immediately and move away."
Shortly after Saree issued the warning, the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV network reported a Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah.
The rebel group said earlier Wednesday that it had carried out two operations targeting the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, as well as the financial center in Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense agency said Tuesday that a skyscraper in the financial district had been targeted by a Houthi attack, injuring 11 people.
U.N. humanitarian chief: Half of Yemen's population needs aid as "renewed fighting" drives displacement

United Nations humanitarian relief chief Tom Fletcher said Wednesday that half of Yemen's population is in need of aid, as he arrived in the war-torn nation that has become the most active front in the intertwined Middle East conflicts.
Fletcher warned in a statement shared online that "renewed fighting has forced over 364,000 people from their homes since August, including tens of thousands this past week alone."

He repeated his demand for Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels to "immediately and unconditionally release " and other humanitarian workers and said the U.N.-led relief efforts in the country were overstretched, underfunded and under attack.

"Yemen is where we are furthest off track on our ambition to reach 87 million people with lifesaving support this year," Fletcher said. "We will not allow the people of Yemen to slip off the world's radar."
Iran claims it has tightened its control over Strait of Hormuz
Iranian army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia said the military had tightened its control and monitoring of the Strait of Hormuz on the orders of the army's commander-in-chief.

Ships attempting to transit the waterway without coordinating with Iran's armed forces have faced greater risks in recent weeks, including sea mines, Akraminia was quoted as saying Wednesday by the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

President Trump has dismissed Iran's claims attacks on ships and sea mines being laid in the strait as lies intended to inflate global energy prices, and the U.S. military international shipping lanes through the waterway free of mines at the end of October.

Without offering any evidence, however, Akraminia claimed Iranian forces had upgraded their monitoring capabilities by introducing new systems, improving existing ones and strengthening their combat abilities, and he said the measures would continue.

Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) said Tuesday that 26 tugboats had been added to the country's "Non-Compliance List," for providing services to non-compliant vessels, indicating they could be targeted.

Iran issues daily claims of commercial vessels striking mines in and near the strait, few of which are ever corroborated, but independent monitors do involving "unknown projectiles" striking ships in the region.
Iran criticizes U.S. for using artificial intelligence for deadly attacks
Iran has denounced the U.S. military's use of to plan and carry out attacks.
Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting Tuesday, Iranian Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi said the weaponization of AI "raises serious concerns."

Darzi claimed U.S. forces used the technology to deploy more than 2,000 munitions to hit 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours. He said Palantir's Maven and Anthropic's system were used to analyze intelligence, identify and prioritize targets and provide strike coordinates.

"Neither advanced technology nor the involvement of private companies can shield the United States or the Israeli regime from accountability for flagrant violations of their obligations under international law," Darzi told the council meeting.

"Those responsible for the commission of atrocious crimes against Iranian people, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian objects, must face individual criminal accountability," he added.

In March 2026, the Commander of U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper confirmed American forces had used a "variety of advanced AI tools" in order to "cut through the noise and make smarter decisions faster than the enemy can react."
While the Pentagon has not said exactly how AI tools are being deployed, CBS News spoke in March with several experts with knowledge of military operations who described the likely scenarios.

"The military is now processing roughly a thousand potential targets a day and striking the majority of them, with turnaround time for the next strike potentially under four hours," said retired Navy Admiral Mark Montgomery, senior director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracy's Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation. "A human is still in the loop, but AI is doing the work that used to take days of analysis — and doing it at a scale no previous campaign has matched."
Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi forces intensify attacks

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Wednesday claimed attacks targeting the financial district in the Saudi capital and the sprawling Ras Tanura refinery in the kingdom's oil-rich east, in retaliation for strikes on their territory.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree described the attack targeting the refinery as "accurate and direct", saying it "caused fires to break out at the facility". He said the attack on Riyadh was "carried out in three phases, with strikes hitting their targets accurately".
In separate attacks, Saudi's forces said they had struck the city of Hodeida on Wednesday, after the Houthis said they would retaliate if that attack took place.

The Houthis have been locked in grueling, more than decade-long civil war against Yemen's government forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. Recent Houthi gains have consolidated the group's control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which the group has tried to use to disrupt Saudi oil exports.
CBS/AFP
Iran developing chemical weapons, Israeli defense minister says, warns of possible preemptive strike
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said in a briefing to Israeli reporters, according to public broadcaster KAN and other national outlets. "The state of Israel will not allow them to reach that capability."
In his briefing on Tuesday, Katz floated the possibility of a preemptive strike against Tehran, if necessary.

"If we recognize that the Iranians intend to attack Israel, can't we tell the army to attack earlier and thwart the threat?" he said, according to a transcript from Israel's Channel 12. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure."

Katz's comments came at the same time as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. government for not funding the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the international body that monitors and combats chemical weapons use at The Hague. The organization is facing a budget crisis because the U.S. has pulled funding, according to a Reuters report.

"The U.S. is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," Araghchi wrote Tuesday on X. "OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs. By obstructing its mandate, the U.S. is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk. Shameful."
The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work in Syria.
CBS/AFP
Jury convicts Chinese tech giant Huawei over business with Iran, other conspiracy charges
A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and doing business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions, including Iran.

In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September.

The Department of Justice said Huawei and its subsidiaries assisted an Iranian intelligence apparatus called Zaeim in monitoring and censoring internet access. The company also provided surveillance cameras that helped Tehran monitor protest activity, according to the DOJ.

"Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the U.S. government that it did not assist Iran's government, military, or intelligence community; that it began restricting its business in Iran in 2011; that Skycom was a business partner, rather than a wholly-owned subsidiary; and that Huawei complied with all applicable sanctions," the DOJ said. "Huawei knew that all of those statements were materially false and misleading."
CBS/AP

articles.headline: Stop eating turkey and start enjoying Thanksgiving
keyFacts: A turkey rescued from becoming meat is celebrated on Thanksgiving at the Gentle Barn animal sanctuary in California in 2025.
| Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images I haven’t eaten turkey in many years, and a large share of Americans who have it on Thanksgiving would rather eat something else , too.
That turkey is the most overrated part of this glorious long weekend between the end of summer and the winter holidays has become a cultural bit as familiar as the dead bird itself.
body: A turkey rescued from becoming meat is celebrated on Thanksgiving at the Gentle Barn animal sanctuary in California in 2025. | Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

I haven’t eaten turkey in many years, and a large share of Americans who have it on Thanksgiving would rather eat something else , too. That turkey is the most overrated part of this glorious long weekend between the end of summer and the winter holidays has become a cultural bit as familiar as the dead bird itself. As the journalist Brian McManus wrote for Vice : “It is, almost without fail, a dried-out, depressing hunk of sun-baked papier-mâché — a jaw-tiringly chewy, unsatisfying, and depressingly bland workout.”

“Throw it in the garbage,” The Guardian commanded about the Thanksgiving turkey a decade ago. That’s indeed what happens to many of them — perhaps their culinary mediocrity is part of why the equivalent of well over 8 million turkeys are thrown away as food waste on Thanksgiving.

This is all very strange, and sad, too, because life is too short to eat bad food on holidays — and the Thanksgiving turkey isn’t a mere harmless tradition. I know it’s untoward and uncool to talk about where our meat comes from at the holiday table, but putting millions of birds through hell for a dish many people can’t stop complaining about seems like a particularly concerning situation.

Turkeys are factory-farmed in the second-largest numbers of any animal in the US, after chickens. Most spend their short lives packed by the thousands into crowded sheds , where the stress can drive them to attack one another; to prevent this, producers cut off parts of their beaks and toes without pain relief. The animals have been bred to grow so large, so fast — their weight has doubled since 1960 — that many struggle to even walk. Like other farmed animals, they don’t even reproduce naturally (more details of how that works on turkey farms, if you can stomach it, can be found here ). The slaughter process is horrific.

I could go on, but surely that’s reason enough to try some different holiday traditions? I have lots of experience cooking and eating on Thanksgiving sans turkey in mixed company (that is, with both committed vegans and lifelong carnivores). Here are some of my favorite, satisfying, crowd-pleasing centerpieces to make instead:
Mushroom Wellington

Everyone was blown away by this plant-based version of a beef Wellington , which my made at last year’s Thanksgiving. It’s a variation on the New York Times’s vegetarian mushroom Wellington . The buttery (yes, even in the vegan version) puff pastry combined with the deep umami and sweet notes of several types of mushrooms and caramelized onions make it a gloriously rich main course that stands on its own and doesn’t feel like a plant-based imitation of something else.

The filling can take quite a bit of time to prepare, but certainly less than the ordeal required to make a turkey taste good. I love the port reduction that accompanies the New York Times version, but it can also be served with a mushroom gravy , a red wine and shallot gravy , or any other sauce you like. Also, if you’re concerned that this is not a very high-protein dish (mushrooms are extremely high in water and aren’t a high-protein food), I promise you’ll get enough protein from the other dishes on the table, and eating one meal without maximizing protein intake won’t do you any harm. But if you do want a protein-packed entrée, there are many options to consider! For this one, I may try adding beans or lentils to the filling in the future.
Creamy lentil bake

I’ve had wonderful experiences making this recipe on holidays . The cashew cream on top, combined with tahini and balsamic flavor in the lentils, make it impossible to stop eating. (Cashew cream, if you’ve never had it, is one of the greatest magic tricks of plant-based cooking.) This lentil shepherd’s pie is a similar concept that’s also excellent and great for those with nut allergies (it does contain sesame, though).
Stuffed squash

I couldn’t make this list without mentioning the option of stuffed squash or pumpkin, a beautiful classic of plant-based holiday fare. I haven’t made one of these in years, but there are endless recipe options online with hundreds of glowing reviews.
Chickpea cutlets

My family has been making these wonderfully firm, dense, chewy patties for many years. Developed by Isa Chandra Moskowitz, the undisputed queen of vegan cooking , the secret to their texture is wheat gluten , which has been used in Asian cuisines for centuries as a meat substitute. Gluten is one of the highest-protein things you can eat — I’m honestly not sure what distinguishes it from protein powder. Definitely serve these with gravy.
Barbecue ribs

For a slightly non-traditional but still distinctly American detour from the usual Thanksgiving flavors, try these plant-based ribs , also made with gluten, by Miyoko Schinner (this same recipe is also found in Schinner’s cookbook, The Homemade Vegan Pantry ). They were so good on the Fourth of July the past few years that we decided to turn them into a Thanksgiving main this year.
Super easy mode: Store-bought plant-based roasts

I know these can be polarizing, but they’ve gotten a lot better since the rubbery meat substitutes of yore. My favorite is Field Roast’s hazelnut and cranberry roast , which is wrapped in flaky puff pastry — kinda like a Wellington — followed by Gardein’s turk’y roast , which has a crispy breaded crust. There are plenty that I haven’t tried too: Juicy Marbles’s whole-cut loin is exceptionally well regarded, though pricey.

My own turkey alternative list is long: I haven’t even gotten to this tried-and-true lentil meatloaf or the creamy baked wild rice with carrots from Nisha Vora’s doorstopper Big Vegan Flavor. For most of us, there’s an extraordinary abundance of food to be grateful for on Thanksgiving — the least we could do is extend a little of that good fortune to turkeys.

articles.headline: Acer Predator Atlas 8 review: Potent performance at a slightly better price
keyFacts: Acer Predator Atlas 8 review: Potent performance at a slightly better price Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival.
Modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home.
But as the category has matured, we've seen manufacturers pursue higher tiers of performance.
body: Acer Predator Atlas 8 review: Potent performance at a slightly better price
Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival.

Modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home. But as the category has matured, we've seen manufacturers pursue higher tiers of performance. This culminated most recently in systems like MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+, which delivers serious graphics power along with an equally serious price of $1,800. But now, Acer is trying to undercut the current framerate champ with the Predator Atlas 8, equipping it with the exact same chip used in MSI's machine, but for $350 less. The result is a compelling package that delivers on many of the same highs while easing the burden on your wallet.
Design and display

With the Predator Atlas 8, Acer hasn't strayed too far from the basic template we've seen on so many other portable PCs. The middle of the system is dominated by a large 8-inch LCD TFT display with a 120Hz refresh and respectable 500-nit brightness. On the outside you get TMR analog sticks along with an Xbox-style button layout. I must admit I'm not a huge fan of Acer's circular D-Pad as it's a bit mushy and doesn't feel super precise. But if you're not playing fighting games or similar titles, it's more than serviceable for navigating menus. And if I'm really nitpicking, colors from the Predator's TFT screen aren't quite as rich as what you get from MSI's machine, but it's the kind of difference that you only really notice when you look at the two systems side by side.

Around back, Acer included a pair of rear paddles, two shoulder buttons and analog Hall-effect triggers with plenty of travel — the latter of which are great for racing games. Along the top edge of the system you get all of the Predator Atlas 8's ports, which includes dual USB-C jacks with support for Thunderbolt 4, a microSD card reader for expandable storage, a 3.5mm audio jack and a power button with a built-in fingerprint reader.

All told, it's a pretty standard setup, though the Predator does lack a USB-A port like you get on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. I also noticed that while Acer's dual two-watt speakers can get surprisingly loud, audio becomes distorted at higher volumes (above 50 TK) that results in a crackly or crunchy sound. That said, the speakers are so punchy, I found that I never really needed to turn them up that high. Unless you're trying to DJ a house party with this thing, you might not even notice.
Performance and software

The real star of the Atlas 8 is its Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor, which is the exact same chip used in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. The main difference is that Acer's handheld comes with 512GB of storage instead of 1TB and tops out with 24GB of shared memory (compared to 32GB on the MSI). This discrepancy almost entirely accounts for the price gap between the two systems. But for people striving for top-notch performance while trying to save a few bucks, the framerate delta in games isn't as pronounced as you might think.

When I tested this out in Cyberpunk 2077 at 35 watts on FHD, medium graphics and XeSS set to performance, the Predator Atlas 8 hit 88 fps, which is barely more than five percent lower than the 95 fps I got from the Claw 8 EX AI+. But it's important to note that this was using Acer's highest performance mode. When I set the system to 15 watts (which you might do when playing on battery only), the Predator and the Claw were essentially dead even in Returnal at FHD and medium graphics (60 fps for the Acer vs 59 fps for the MSI). This means that if you're trying to decide between the two, you really need to consider how you plan on using your handheld and what types of games you'll be playing.

Similar to other high-end Windows handhelds, the Atlas 8 comes with Microsoft's Xbox experience. This software allows you to boot into a dedicated UI for gaming instead of needing to deal with the traditional desktop OS. This also makes it super easy to download all of the most popular launchers and storefronts like Epic, Steam, Battle.net and more, and because it's Windows underneath, you get better compatibility than what you get from SteamOS-powered portables. That said, if you're the type to travel with a portable monitor, keyboard and mouse, you can still switch over to the classic Windows interface to get some work done too.
Battery life

The Atlas 8 is powered by an 80WHr battery that provides ample longevity, though it can vary quite a bit depending on what you're playing. However, without even doing anything to boost its longevity, I was able to play World of Warcraft: Forever at FHD on medium settings for an hour and 45 minutes on a single charge while still keeping frame rates consistently above 90. On the flipside, when I played a less demanding title like Warhammer Survivors, Acer's machine had more battery life than I knew what to do with: It lasted for more than three hours before needing to be plugged in. Notably, both of those games were played using the handheld's 30-watt Balanced performance mode, so if you're not afraid to mess around with its settings, there's a lot of room to tweak this thing to get even longer untethered gaming sessions.
Wrap-up

I'm still not sure how I feel about PC handhelds that cost well above $1,000. For me, that's just a ton of money to drop on a system that can't multitask as well as a similarly priced gaming laptop. However, for mobile gaming enthusiasts trying to find the sweet spot between price, performance and portability, Acer has carved out an interesting niche with the Predator Atlas 8.

At $1,450, it costs $350 less than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, while sporting the exact same processor and delivering essentially 95 percent of the performance. That said, Acer's more approachable pricing leaves the Predator with a bit less RAM and storage, though having a microSD card slot provides a workaround for the latter. There are also some minor differences, like the lack of a USB-A port, a slightly less colorful TFT display and speakers that sound a bit wonky at high volumes. But these shortcomings could very well be a worthwhile trade-off for anyone looking for peak handheld gaming performance without completely fragging their budget.

articles.headline: Zelda Producers: Ocarina of Time Remake Is a Bridge to the Future
keyFacts: Over the last month, I fell in love with a new game that’s actually old.
It’s happened to me before, but Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake drove that feeling home in a surprising way.
How did Nintendo get me to fall so deeply in love again with a game I’ve already played?
body: Over the last month, I fell in love with a new game that’s actually old. It’s happened to me before, but Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake drove that feeling home in a surprising way. How did Nintendo get me to fall so deeply in love again with a game I’ve already played? And why is it still winning me over, even with Grand Theft Auto 6 here?

I’m still thinking about (and playing) Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2, even with GTA 6 loaded up at home. GTA’s universe overwhelms me, but it also makes me appreciate Ocarina’s focus and clarity. And it’s also another incredible graphics showcase for what the Switch 2 is capable of. Yes, GTA 6 is jaw-dropping. But so are Ocarina’s 60fps vistas and details. Zelda pioneered 3D gaming before GTA ever went 3D.

I also can’t stop thinking about what a game like this means for Nintendo’s next wave of Switch 2 games, and a future Zelda game. Zelda’s previous games became increasingly open world, full of multiplying tasks and larger maps. It can get overwhelming. Ocarina of Time’s focus is smaller, but still tangled and immersive. Can the two concepts feed off each other? Will Ocarina help rethink where the next Zeldas are heading? And, maybe, where other open-world games are heading, too?
More from CNET

At Ocarina’s launch, I met in person with Nintendo’s producers for the remake, Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, to discuss what it all meant and how the remake bridged the gap between the “old Zelda” and “new Zelda.” Aonuma has been a producer for Zelda games since the original Ocarina of Time, and Fujibayashi directed both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.
For this project, they brought on staffers who’d worked on Tears of the Kingdom, many of them much younger developers.

“In fact, some of them hadn’t even played the original Ocarina of Time on Nintendo 64,” says Aonuma. “We also saw this as a really interesting opportunity for this younger staff to make discoveries on the course of this project that they could bring forward on future Zelda projects that they might work on as well.”
There are a lot more subtle visual clues, I found, even than what I remembered in Nintendo’s last two Zelda games.

“When we were working on Tears of the Kingdom, we had this very high capacity to express all kinds of details and this feeling of immersion in the world, and that’s something I think was a big influence on the remake,” says Aonuma. “Whether it’s a visual detail that you might spot from a distance that you may not have in the original, that could be something that draws the player in and suddenly gives them the motivation to explore.”
What worked wonders, I found, was the quiet, subtle immersion, especially when exploring dungeons or figuring out solutions I’d forgotten decades ago. I had to study the environment for clues.
That’s the magic ingredient: a throughline in the Zelda games that Fujibayashi says is “the idea of exploration and discovery.”
Fujibayashi appreciates how the visual tools have improved, even since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom on the original Switch.

“A system that lets you share a high, dense volume of information visually provides new ways of giving clues to the player: They can use their sight to gather the information they need to do some of the puzzle solving,” he says. “Even if you compare the graphics to Breath of the Wild, it looks slightly more realistic now. And that impacts how we approach puzzle solving and puzzle creation.”

I think about Grand Theft Auto as the new benchmark for immersion and graphic detail, but I’m also finding that a lot of GTA’s discoveries are made through pop-up interaction graphics that let you know when something can be activated. Ocarina of Time doesn’t always do this. And I also can’t help but wonder: Could the Switch 2 achieve a way to run a new wave of impressive games using optimized graphics, even something on a level like Grand Theft Auto’s latest?
Or, rather, what if Nintendo aims for a new level of hyper-immersion in its games going forward, learning from Ocarina of Time?

Speaking of immersion, I kind of wish I could hold my Joy-Con up and use it like an ocarina in the new game. You can’t, although you can use the controllers to play notes or hum or play a tune into the built-in microphone using your own voice or instrument — something lots of people have been showing off online. But the Joy-Con-as-ocarina idea almost became a reality.

“To be honest, we did briefly think about doing exactly that, but then we also considered how difficult it is to turn the Joy-Con into something that’s going to make a sound that is faithful, and then also how to develop that into the application inside of the game as well,” says Aonuma. “What we ultimately decided to do instead was to have this audio recognition feature in the software where you can use any instrument that you would like, whether it’s analog or digital, and you can play these themes and have the effect in the game and experience that way.”

What I’m really hoping for is a Majora’s Mask remake, the second N64 Zelda game that built off Ocarina’s graphics engine. Nintendo could do the same here, although Nintendo wouldn’t answer my questions about Majora’s Mask during my interview.

I’m still unlocking all the little secrets in Ocarina of Time, sinking into the world as I go. And when I play the notes on my Switch, I imagine I’m playing that ocarina. After playing this Zelda game, I wonder what Nintendo could do with that same level of detail for Mario’s return on the Switch 2, almost 10 years after the last new 3D Mario game on the Switch. We might know the answer to that soon enough.

articles.headline: Tangles Review
keyFacts: Tangles is in theaters in New York and Los Angeles on Nov.
It will expand to a wider release in January.
The weight of memory is vital to the biographical animated feature Tangles, a black-and-white story about family, the queer ‘90s, and above all else, early-onset Alzheimer’s.
body: Tangles is in theaters in New York and Los Angeles on Nov. 27. It will expand to a wider release in January.

The weight of memory is vital to the biographical animated feature Tangles, a black-and-white story about family, the queer ‘90s, and above all else, early-onset Alzheimer’s. Based on the sparse but powerful 2012 comic by Sarah Leavitt — who co-wrote the screenplay with Trev Renney and director Leah Nelson — the film employs abstractions in its margins and connective tissue, making room for straightforward drama that proves incredibly moving in its unearthing of lived experience.

Beginning with a childhood flashback, Tangles introduces us to middle-aged Midge (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), based on Leavitt’s mother, as she helps a young Sarah (Fern Grandin) fight invisible monsters in her bedroom, with the help of a flashlight which Sarah imagines as a fuchsia lightsaber. Midge is, for all intents and purposes, Sarah’s superhero, but life goes on as the film skips forward to 1999. The adult Sarah, voiced by Abbi Jacobson, draws for a queer magazine in San Francisco, but a return to her hometown for a family visit proves a major turning point. Everyone including Sarah’s soft-spoken father Rob (Bryan Cranston), her idiosyncratic aunts Debbie (Pamela Adlon) and Sukey (Sarah Silverman) and her lively sister Hannah (Beanie Feldstein) seems to dance around major changes in Midge’s lifestyle and cognitive function.

They blame it, at first, on menopause, and then on Midge losing her job and her ensuing depression, but minor tasks prove frustrating and confusing for the usually gentle 50-something, who’s drawn with appropriately haggard squiggles. It takes a while before a real diagnosis tells them what might be wrong: an early form of dementia. This forces Sarah to fly back and forth between her family and her supportive, stud girlfriend Donimo (Samira Wiley), a schism of time, place and culture that slowly wears on her as Midge’s disease advances.

The dynamic between Sarah’s queer, urban environment and her nominally accepting but high-strung Jewish family allows the film to traverse different modes of expression and conversational rhythm, as she tries to be in two places at once. This dichotomy also helps enhance periods of nerve-wracking transition during lengthy travel, expressed through tongue-in-cheek formal flourishes. Each flight, for instance, becomes the venue for dreamlike jokes about Sarah’s deep-seated anxieties delivered over the plane’s PA system, leaving her vulnerable and exposed.

Louis-Dreyfus delivers a heartrending, piercingly realistic vocal performance as a woman trying to hold on to what little of herself she can find. Sarah is a character perpetually on edge, a baseline made all the more volatile when she takes it upon herself to recognize her mother’s illness and care for her as best she can, even at the cost of her various relationships. Midge, meanwhile, slips away gradually over the film’s 102 minutes, as Louis-Dreyfus delivers a heartrending, piercingly realistic vocal performance as a woman trying to hold on to what little of herself she can find.

The period setting is rendered with appropriate details — a few too many Marvel references aside, it feels like a sketched memory of the late 1990s, from pop culture to the textures and technologies — but the story itself is timeless. Nelson brings Leavitt’s autobiographical tale to life with generosity, imbuing each supporting character with a palpable denial that feels, at first, like a mere quirk, before revealing itself to be a coping mechanism. The gradual confusion and anger involved (both for Midge and her caretakers) results in a moving portrait of helplessness in the face of a brutal disease, as well as the few moments of love people are able to steal from it while they still can. By the time the film wraps up, its echoes of Midge in earlier scenes continue to loom large thanks to Louis-Dreyfus’ fine-tuned performance as she leaves quiet gaps in her wake, alongside a sense of longing for the character she used to be.

articles.headline: Wait, What? GTA 6 Runs Better On Xbox Series X Than PS5
keyFacts: When it comes toÂ GTA 6, PlayStation has very much been the teacher’s pet.
Microsoft has had a weird-ass ban on even mentioning that the game was coming out on its console, while the PS5 has been broadly promoted as the natural home for Rockstar’s record-breaking release.
And yet,Â Digital Foundry‘s latest analysis ofÂ GTA 6‘s performance across all four of Microsoft and Sony’s current-gen systems shows the Series X outdoing the PS5.
body: When it comes toÂ GTA 6, PlayStation has very much been the teacher’s pet. Microsoft has had a weird-ass ban on even mentioning that the game was coming out on its console, while the PS5 has been broadly promoted as the natural home for Rockstar’s record-breaking release. And yet,Â Digital Foundry‘s latest analysis ofÂ GTA 6‘s performance across all four of Microsoft and Sony’s current-gen systems shows the Series X outdoing the PS5. “Ultimately,” the site’s boffins report, “Series X is meaningfully better off.”

It’s important to mention right away that the PS5 Pro still wipes the floor with the Series X, and is without doubt the best way to play Grand Theft Auto VI until the official PC version is released. But when you measure the two base machines between the rival console makers,Â DF says there’s no doubt that it’s the Series X that edges ahead of the PS5.

Both consoles offer “a virtually identical visual presentation,” say the tech experts, with nothing to divide them in all the important areas. But when it comes to performance, this is where Xbox takes the lead. Both machines struggle during “heavy vehicle traversal” and “intense airport crowd sequences,” but the PS5 “suffers substantially more frequent frame-rate drops” than the Series X, “which is compounded by the fact that the Xbox machine also benefits from 120Hz VRR support to smooth out minor dips.”

Unsurprisingly, the Series S performs the poorest out of all four, but actually offers better results than anyone was expecting. While its framerate drops are horrible, frequently dipping into the teens, the use of PSR 4.1 upscaling and a reduction in the most intensive details still has it looking pretty lovely. It’s definitely not a great way to play the game, but it’s less terrible than you’d think.

So there you go, Xbox owners: you’re not the ugly step-sister you might have been made to feel. Obviously the differences remain slight, and with both consoles (and even the PS5 Pro) capped to 30 FPS there are compromises to be made by all, so whether you’re playing on PlayStation or Xbox Series X, you’re mostly having the same experience. But Xbox owners have earned themselves a quietly smug grin.

articles.headline: Please, GTA 6, Give Us More of Jason’s Favorite Gay Romantasy Series
keyFacts: Jason Duval is a pretty quiet guy, as far as Grand Theft Auto protagonists go, but there's more to this character than meets the eye, including his love of books.
In GTA 6, players will find several books scattered around Jason and Lucia's home in Key Lento, such as Ashes of Glory, Lethal by Design, and Orca, A Whole Different Animal.
They can interact with each book to add it to their collection.
body: Jason Duval is a pretty quiet guy, as far as Grand Theft Auto protagonists go, but there's more to this character than meets the eye, including his love of books. In GTA 6, players will find several books scattered around Jason and Lucia's home in Key Lento, such as Ashes of Glory, Lethal by Design, and Orca, A Whole Different Animal. They can interact with each book to add it to their collection. Unfortunately, they can't pick up The Battle for Zantoroth, the book on his nightstand.

Thankfully, Jason actually carries it around and reads it at the beach, giving players the chance to sneak a look at it. As it turns out, The Battle for Zantoroth is the second book in the in-game King of Gorgollia romantasy series. Hey, who's to say that a hardened criminal can't enjoy a romantasy book? It's a popular genre for a reason.
Jason Duval is hooked on a gay incest romantasy series

The blurb on the back cover gives us a good idea of the plot of the book. The Battle for Zantoroth is about Austin Livingstone, a man who works in a tavern, who is sent by the king on a harsh journey out to sea alongside Jonathan "Sticky Broom" Ritchey, a sailor and tavern regular. As the two embark on the voyage, they come across a plethora of dangers and challenges that ultimately bring them closer. Eventually, the lines between friendship and lust become blurred. They come to learn that they are not just lovers, but actually... father and son. At this point, they have gone too far, and it is too late to turn back.

The description and accessible content of the book highlight the intensity of its author, Timothy D. D. Ewell, "former plastic surgeon and part-time self-defense instructor." The plot is certainly something, so it's no surprise that the King of Gorgollia series gained a cult following in the fictional world of GTA 6 and led to several award-winning TV and film adaptations.

It is unknown how Jason got his hands on this book, whether it was a present from a friend or whether he wanted to supportthe Men for Women's Rights, since 3% of the proceeds go to this foundation, confirming Jason truly is the perfect boyfriend. Regardless, he keeps it by his nightstand, brings it to the beach, and is already on book two of the series, which suggests he's already somewhat invested. Hopefully, we'll come across more entries in the series at some point in the game.

articles.headline: Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
keyFacts: Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays.

body: Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories

The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

- 🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

- 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

- 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.
Today's listen

NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.
There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.
Life advice

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.
- 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"

- 🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.
- 🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.
- 🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.
For more guidance on how to switch off your work brain, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

articles.headline: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
keyFacts: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem.
He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer.
He had actually solved this particular problem already.
body: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics.

LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

They asked other physicists for some of their private gems—minor but real findings they’d never gotten around to cleaning up for public display. They were asking for real work, problems that take humans at the top of the field about a day to solve.
“Our contributors had to either sacrifice potential publication elsewhere, or else undertake a small research project just for us,” Raju wrote.

By the time all the questions and answers were ready, the AIs were, too. At a colloquium in September, Raju shared preliminary results showing that leading AI models could solve about 60 percent of the problems on their own. And by the time he and his colleagues finished the full set, the situation had advanced further: GPT-6 Astra could solve nearly 90 percent of the problems.

Flame/Ice are excellent ranged options to ragdoll Poison damage is high and easy to land with Predator Crush Best of all you have insane sustain with the healing arrow and add a good weapon for added DPS for a strong build

articles.headline: GTA 6's best lore drops happen when you're chilling with your partner, so stop leaving them at home all the time
keyFacts: My real relationship be damned, this last week has been all about playing cupid in Grand Theft Auto 6.
I've become utterly invested in keeping Jason and Lucia in love, which means a lot of my time in the game has been spent doing things with my partner in tow.
Hitting the gym, inviting them out for a late-night bite, robbing a few jewellery stores.
body: My real relationship be damned, this last week has been all about playing cupid in Grand Theft Auto 6. I've become utterly invested in keeping Jason and Lucia in love, which means a lot of my time in the game has been spent doing things with my partner in tow. Hitting the gym, inviting them out for a late-night bite, robbing a few jewellery stores. You know, couple things. Things couples do.

And, as people tend to do when they're spending a lot of time together, Jason and Lucia talk. A lot. And you know what? Some of the best nuggets of information about their lives—both their time spent together before the events of the game, and their own individual lives before meeting one another—are tucked away in these interactions that fill the game's quieter moments.

Sometimes the interactions are simply fluffy, or funny. Lucia poking fun at Jason for his deep voice and monosyllabic responses, or them reminiscing about little moments that happened in their relationship before the whole "Lucia ghosting Jason and ending up in jail" thing. Sometimes it's Lucia getting a spam call and giving the bot (and eventual human) on the other end of the phone an absolute earful.

But then, occasionally, beyond all the comedic conversations and flavour dialogue that give these characters so much life, the game'll drop some proper good lore. I'll do my best not to spoil stuff here, but for almost every complaint I've seen on social media about why certain protagonists did certain things, there's an answer tucked away in these interactions. The kind of things you'd really want to know about these characters? Your best chance of finding it all out is when you bring them together.

I've really enjoyed having lore drops unfold in mundane conversations while walking around, driving, or eating a burger, rather than hamfisted into the main story. They feel like natural breathing moments for the couple to recount the past, or get into the stuff that was happening in the time that they were apart. You know, the exact kind of times actual couples and friends would find the time to dig into these things in real life, too.

That doesn't mean you have to keep them together all the time. Some of their exclusive missions also provide a great bit of insight into their backstories—like Jason's side stuff with ex-army pal Bret Vogel, or the missions that have Lucia in some all-too-real situations with her mother.

I've played plenty of the game flying solo as both protagonists too, and you'll occasionally get some of this nattering just by hanging around in your abode together. But I can't recommend enough that you find plenty of opportunities to bring them together out in the open world. Even if it's just for 15 minutes here and there, you'll uncover a whole lot about who they were before we first got to know them as the player. And as someone who has really enjoyed learning just about everything about these two as I can, it's been one of my favourite parts of the game so far.

body: As Republicans continue to pick up the pieces from their 2026 midterm losses, one Trump administration official is catching some GOP lawmakers' eyes as the party's next great hope.

"[Secretary of State Marco Rubio] is the whole package. He's intelligent, charismatic, level-headed, cool-tempered and very knowledgeable about the issues and eloquent in explaining them," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "I think there is a lot of interest from Republicans in seeing him explore a run."

Indeed, multiple House Republicans who spoke with Fox News Digital said they and their colleagues are pushing Rubio to run for president in 2028. The Cabinet official himself has publicly dismissed any talk about his future political plans, but his name is on the rise among Republicans who have said the party needs to pivot from the issues that cost them votes in November.
HOUSE CONSERVATIVE EMERGES WITH 2028 PRESIDENTIAL PICK AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'I AM ALL IN'

"Now that we lost majorities, we can't push policy, so we will have to do better at communicating," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital on election night. "I am all in for Marco. He can be a unifier."
They're notable comments coming from the Indiana Republican, who was among the founding members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus.
MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028
Rubio has long been held up as a potential 2028 contender, despite a previous unsuccessful White House bid in 2016.

He and Vice President JD Vance have been regarded as the top contenders for the GOP nomination, but it's Rubio's name that has come up in conversations among House Republicans, Fox News Digital was told.
GOP MIDTERM BLOODBATH EXPOSES CRACKS IN VANCE'S 2028 WHITE HOUSE AMBITIONS

"A number of my colleagues, unsolicited by me — they come up with me, knowing that I'm on board, [from] Miami, et cetera — and said that they'd want to support him, that they would support him if he ran," Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. " And it's not just a few. There's a number, a pretty good number, that have told me that."

Gimenez said he supported Rubio even before the election. The same goes for Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., who told Fox News Digital he's been openly backing his fellow Florida Republican for two months.
"And I think the affirmation that I'm getting from talking to people is overwhelming," Haridopolos said.

"He is not only understanding what's happening today, but our place in history. And I think his inspirational story, his parents coming from Cuba and living the opportunity that is America, and inspiring people that anything is possible is the uplifting message we need."
SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM

Both Haridopolos and Malliotakis pointed to Rubio's recent speech in Greece calling for the renewal of Western civilization as an example of his presidential possibility. Those remarks, set in Athens, were widely lauded for their scenic backdrop of the Acropolis at sunset.
And Malliotakis, who is half Cuban herself, said Rubio could "reach" Hispanic voters who largely turned away from the GOP in November.
LATINO VOTERS SWING BACK TO DEMOCRATS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS: POLL
"The potential for him to be the first Hispanic president is huge for our party and the country," she said.
But within the administration itself, it appears no clear successor has emerged.
One source familiar with talks told Fox News Digital that Trump administration staffers were "about 50/50" when asked if they favored Vance or Rubio .
"I think it’s pretty split," one administration official said. "I don’t think the president really knows. I think if you asked him today, he’d say Rubio."
"50/50 feels right to me," a second administration official said.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly referred Fox News Digital to President Donald Trump’s previous comments on the matter.

Over the weekend, Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that Vance and Rubio are "doing fantastically" and are "both very, very popular" when asked who he would like to see run on the Republican and Democratic tickets ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for comment but did not hear back by press time.

articles.headline: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
keyFacts: A US jury found Huawei guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud, and sanctions violations, but acquitted it of racketeering.
Federal prosecutors stated that Huawei spent decades using lies and theft to gain a competitive business advantage and expand globally.
Huawei plans to seek the lowest possible sentence in September 2027 and fully expects to appeal the guilty verdicts.
body: - Published
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.
"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

articles.headline: A New Court Decision Gives Trump Another Shot At Erasing His Criminal Conviction
keyFacts: On Monday, a three-judge panel for the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, issued a brief order finding that U.S.
District Judge Alvin Hellerstein — a Clinton appointee who died in October — “erred” when denying Trump’s second request to remove his case from the New York state courts to a federal court.
Hellerstein had ruled in August that because Trump had been both convicted and sentenced, the case could not be transferred to federal courts.
body: On Monday, a three-judge panel for the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, issued a brief order finding that U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein — a Clinton appointee who died in October — “erred” when denying Trump’s second request to remove his case from the New York state courts to a federal court.

Hellerstein had ruled in August that because Trump had been both convicted and sentenced, the case could not be transferred to federal courts. The appeals panel, comprised of U.S. Circuit Judges Raymond Lohier, an Obama appointee, John Walker, a George H.W. Bush appointee, and Jose Cabranes, a Clinton appointee, disagreed. They also disagreed with Hellerstein’s earlier ruling finding that Trump lacked “good cause” to try to remove the case again.
The case now goes to the Southern District of New York, where a new judge will preside.

Trump was found guilty in 2024 of 34 counts of falsifying business records to conceal a hush money payment made to adult film actor Stormy Daniels ahead of the 2016 presidential election. He formally appealed the conviction last year, but the conviction remains intact as litigation continues.

Trump’s lawyers have been pushing hard to have the conviction erased and moved to federal court. They argue the process, known as “removal,” is necessary because the actions he took around the payments were “official” duties, and official duties related to core powers of the president are covered from prosecution under the Supreme Court’s immunity decision in Trump v. United States.

According to Courthouse News Service, lawyers for New York state argued at a hearing this month that Trump twice had his chance to make the immunity arguments when attempting to remove the case, but had failed to do so in a timely manner.
When Hellerstein rejected Trump’s request to move the criminal case to federal court in August, he didn’t mince words about his decision. Trump’s arguments were not novel, new or valid, he ruled.
“Paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity,” Hellerstein wrote.

Though convicted by a jury of 34 felony counts, Trump did not receive a prison sentence or punishment even though the felonies, classified as “class E” felonies, typically carry a penalty of up to four years in prison per count. Instead, last January and after winning the 2024 presidential race, he received what is known as an “unconditional discharge.” Judge Juan Merchan, who presided over the criminal trial and issued Trump’s sentence, said the discharge was “the most viable” and “only lawful sentence” permitted given the Supreme Court’s immunity ruling.
Trump’s lawyers responded to the ruling, calling it “prompt and correct,” and said Trump would continue to “win” against “Democrat weaponization of the Justice System.”
